## Front Country Camping

There are more than 250 front country campgrounds that offer a range of facilities from basic campsites, to full hookups, in walk-in tenting, group campsites, individual campsites and comfort camping.

![](https://www.albertaparks.ca/media/6496920/individual-campsites.jpg)

#### Individual Campsites

- Accommodates one camping accommodation unit per campsite.
- An additional full camping fee may be charged for a second unit.

[Online Reservations](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/camping-in-alberta-parks/online-reservations/) [First-Come,\\
\\
First-Served](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/camping-in-alberta-parks/first-come-first-served/)

![](https://www.albertaparks.ca/media/6496919/group-camping.jpg)

#### Group Camping

- [Group camping areas](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/camping-in-alberta-parks/group-camping-areas/) and [group day use areas](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/day-use/).
- Ideal for company and club functions, family reunions, and other special events.

[Explore](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/camping-in-alberta-parks/group-camping-areas/)

![](https://www.albertaparks.ca/media/6496916/comfort-camping.jpg)

#### Comfort Camping

- [Comfort camping](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/camping-in-alberta-parks/comfort-camping/) is an easy, convenient alternative.
- [Comfort camping rules](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/camping-in-alberta-parks/comfort-camping/rules-for-comfort-camping-reservations/)

[Explore](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/camping-in-alberta-parks/comfort-camping/)

![](https://www.albertaparks.ca/media/6496922/walk-in-tenting.jpg)

#### Walk-in Tenting

- Walk-in tenting campsites are accessible by foot; they are located a short distance from the nearest parking area.
- These sites are noted in the details for each campground.


[Explore](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/camping-in-alberta-parks/walk-in-tenting/ "Walk-in Tenting")

![](https://www.albertaparks.ca/media/6496918/equestrian-camping.jpg)

#### Equestrian Camping

- [Equestrian campgrounds](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/camping-in-alberta-parks/equestrian-camping/ "Equestrian Camping") are equipped with such facilities as hitching rails, horse corrals and loading ramps.
- Most equestrian campgrounds are auto-accessible but a few are located in the backcountry.

[Explore](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/camping-in-alberta-parks/equestrian-camping/ "Equestrian Camping")

![](https://www.albertaparks.ca/media/6496915/winter-camping.jpg)

#### Fall, Winter and Spring Camping

- Some campgrounds stay open year-round and offer [Fall, Winter and Spring camping](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/camping-in-alberta-parks/fall-winter-and-spring-camping/ "Fall, Winter and Spring Camping").
- Check out our [Time to Relax in Alberta's Provincial Parks](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/learning/parks-blog/fall-and-winter-camping-in-provincial-parks/ "Fall and Winter Camping in Provincial Parks") story for more details on camping in fall or winter.


[Explore](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/camping-in-alberta-parks/fall-winter-and-spring-camping/ "Fall, Winter and Spring Camping")

## Everyone Belongs Outside!

Alberta’s parks are important to our quality of life and we are committed to making parks more accessible and inclusive so that everyone benefits from outdoor recreation and spending time in nature. A priority of the [Plan for Parks](https://www.albertaparks.ca/media/123436/p4p.pdf "Plan for Parks (2009)") is to implement a province-wide inclusion plan to enhance visitor experiences. [Everyone Belongs Outside: Alberta Parks Inclusion Plan](https://www.albertaparks.ca/media/5143694/everyone-belongs-outside.pdf "Alberta Parks Inclusion Plan: Everyone Belongs Outside (2014)") was released in response. Alberta Parks has been working on ensuring facilities and programs are designed so that everyone’s needs are considered regardless of age, ability or disability, economic standing or other factors.

## Our Goals

- **Improving Access**

Accessibility means identifying and removing barriers through design, auditing parks and training for Alberta Parks staff. The primary goal here is to find ways to improve access in sites and experiences across Alberta’s network of parks.

- **Inviting Participation**

It takes time to develop relationships. Moving beyond access and inviting participation requires an open mind, time and patience.

- **Increasing Capacity**

Capacity building strategies will build the programs we have and provide opportunities to collaborate. Removing barriers and increasing capacity means more people can benefit from connecting to the natural world.

## Push to Open Nature

The [Push to Open Nature Initiative](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/inclusion-and-accessibility/push-to-open-nature/ "Push to Open Nature") seeks to breaks down physical and mental barriers to nature. The goals are to improve accessibility and promote inclusion of all abilities through adaptive recreation events and partners.

## Nature as a Second Language

The goal of the [Nature as a Second Language Initiative](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/inclusion-and-accessibility/nature-as-a-second-language/ "Nature as a Second Language") is to remove language barriers and introduce newcomers to outdoor recreation and to provincial parks. The "Introduction to Alberta's Provincial Parks" guidebook and regulations brochure are available in several languages.

## Canoo App

Alberta Parks, together with the [Institute for Canadian Citizenship](https://forcitizenship.ca/), supports new citizens to discover Canadian culture and Alberta's provincial parks with the mobile [Canoo App](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparksca/visit-our-parks/inclusion-and-accessibility/canoo-app/). We invite you to get outside and make memories at nearly 500 parks across Alberta.

## Camping Options

Alberta Parks has accessible sites located at various parks and recreation areas around the province. Please visit our [Accessible Camping](https://www.albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/camping-in-alberta-parks/online-reservations/accessible-camping/ "Accessible Camping") page to learn more.

Alberta Parks has lots of camping options that offer varied experiences at price points beginning at $0. Please check our [Low Cost Camping Options](https://albertaparks.ca/albertaparks-ca/visit-our-parks/camping-in-alberta-parks/low-cost-camping-options/ "Low Cost Camping Options") page for details.

, [Site 5A Group Use](https://www.albertaparks.ca/parks/north/beaver-lake-pra/information-facilities/group-use/site-5a/)
, [Site 5B Group Use](https://www.albertaparks.ca/parks/north/beaver-lake-pra/information-facilities/group-use/site-5b/)

**Details:**

Please be advised that Cyanobacterial (Blue-Green Algae) has been identified in the water at this location. Additional information can be found online at [AHS Health Advisories](https://www.albertahealthservices.ca/news/Page1926.aspx)

Visitors are advised to take the following precautions:

- Avoid all contact with cyanobacterial blooms. If contact occurs, wash with tap water as soon as possible.
- Do not swim or wade or allow your pets to swim or wade in any areas where cyanobacteria is visible.
- Do not feed whole fish or fish trimmings from this lake to your pets.
- Consider limiting human consumption of whole fish and fish trimmings from this lake, as it is known that fish may store toxins in their liver. People can safely consume fish fillets from this lake.

As always, visitors and residents are reminded to never drink or cook with untreated water directly from any recreational body of water at any time. **Boiling this water will not remove the toxins produced by cyanobacteria.** An alternative source of drinking water should also be provided for pets and livestock while this advisory is active.

Weather and wind conditions can cause algae blooms to move from one location in the lake to another. As such, this advisory will remain in effect until further notice.

_Please note:_ Waters in which the cyanobacterial bloom is **NOT** visible can still be used for recreational purposes, even while this Health Advisory is in place.

## ![](https://www.albertaparks.ca/media/rquffqvk/warning-icon-red.svg)**Construction Closure** – Quaite Valley Backcountry Campground

**Effective Date:**
September 28, 2026

\- Until Further Notice



**Where:** [Bow Valley Wildland Provincial Park](https://www.albertaparks.ca/parks/kananaskis/bow-valley-wpp/)
, [Quaite Valley Backcountry Campground](https://www.albertaparks.ca/parks/kananaskis/bow-valley-wpp/information-facilities/camping/quaite-valley-backcountry/)

**Details:**

Please be advised that Alberta Parks will be doing construction work at Quaite Valley Backcountry Campground beginning September 28, 2026. Construction crews will be on site working to upgrade the backcountry campground.

To support construction activities, Alberta Parks is closing the campground for the following reasons:

- To reduce danger to backcountry campers as contractors work in the area falling trees and moving heavy equipment.
- It is more time and cost effective. The contractor needs to be able to work efficiently without keeping track of the public in the campground. Alberta Forestry and Parks wants to complete the project as efficiently as possible.

Please note:

- Quaite Creek Trail is anticipated to remain open throughout the project.
- Alternative backcountry camping opportunities during any closure period include Elbow Lake Backcountry Campground, Point Backcountry Campground, and Jewell Bay Backcountry Campground, subject to current road conditions, trail closures, and advisories.
- Visitors are encouraged to check current conditions before travelling to the area.

Follow the direction of all signage and personnel in the area and stay out of active construction zones.

## ![](https://www.albertaparks.ca/media/x32d4wlp/caution-icon-color.svg)**Fecal Water Quality** – Calling Lake

**Effective Date:**
August 27, 2026

\- Until Further Notice



**Where:** [Calling Lake Provincial Park](https://www.albertaparks.ca/parks/north/calling-lake-pp/)

**Details:**

The water at this location is tested weekly by Alberta Health Services. Our most recent test has produced fecal indicator bacteria levels that exceed the recommended limits. Additional information can be found online at [AHS Health Advisories](https://www.albertahealthservices.ca/news/Page1926.aspx)

Contact with these waters may cause illness, and swimming is not recommended.

Never drink or cook with untreated water directly from any lake or reservoir, at any time. Water-borne organisms, including fecal bacteria, can cause vomiting and diarrhea.

For more information on beach monitoring, please contact Alberta Health Services at **811**.
